title: The Name carries across
hookLine: the Name is the boat across the world's ocean (Salok M9, ang 1428)
last: HEAD SHAKES — TURN WHILE YOU CAN.

cards: It's three in the morning, and the worry has arrived. Money, a test result, a child far away, the thing you said that you can't unsay. The room is dark and the thoughts are loud.
Each one pulls you further out, like a swimmer caught in a current, and the shore keeps getting smaller. Thinking harder doesn't get anyone out. In this picture, thinking is the water.
What you need is something that floats. Gurbani has an old answer for this, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks reach for it again and again.

teach.b: Across the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is pictured as an ocean: bhav saagar, the ocean of existence, sometimes bhau nidh, the terrifying sea.
It's deep and full of waves: desire, fear, grief, the endless round of coming and going. In Gurbani's picture, nobody swims it on their own strength.

The way across is the Name, Naam, the remembrance of the Lord, pictured as a boat. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the call keeps coming: says Nanak, O mind, meditate on the Lord, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean.
We heard it at the end of the salok about the Lord in every heart. Notice what a boat is. It doesn't empty the ocean.
The waves stay. The storm can still come. But you're carried on top of it instead of pulled under.
Sikhs use this picture for simran. The worries at three in the morning don't vanish when someone repeats Waheguru; what Sikhs describe is having something under them now.
Think back to Makhan Shah, at the start of this block. Tradition says that when his ship was caught in a storm, he turned to the Guru, and the ship came through.
Sikhs tell that story as history and as a picture at the same time: in Sikh teaching, the Name keeps a person afloat while the storm passes.
And a boat has one more lesson: you have to get in.
In the saloks, the one who crosses is the one who remembers, who actually says the Name, especially in the worried hour.

how: Many Sikhs repeat Waheguru, quietly or aloud, in moments of fear or worry, and speak of the Name as the boat across the world's ocean, an image found throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the Name, remembering the Lord, a boat across
a sacred text read only in the gurdwara
a person's own name, said with pride

games.q: the Name carries across — tap the pairs.

s: the boat image means the Name makes the waves disappear
the waves stay; the boat carries you on top of them.
Gurbani pictures the world as an ocean
bhav saagar, the ocean of existence, sometimes bhau nidh, the terrifying sea.
admiring the boat from the shore is enough to cross
you have to get in: the Name carries those who actually say it.

games.q: it's three in the morning and worry is pulling you out like a current. what do the saloks offer?
o: swim harder: think it all through.
the Name, the boat that carries you across.
wait for the ocean to dry up.
games.why: says Nanak, O mind, meditate on the Lord, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. the waves stay; the Name keeps you afloat.

practice: Let one current worry come up, feel where it sits in the body, and don't try to solve it. If you pray, say Waheguru slowly, once on the in-breath and once on the out-breath; if you don't, rest on one steady word, like here.
Let the worry stay, and notice that something is holding you up while it does.

wordCard.voice: Naam, the Name, the remembrance of the Lord. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the world is a terrifying ocean, and naam is the boat that carries you over the waves.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Naam, the Name, the remembrance of the Lord, pictured as the boat across.

carryVoice: Your line: the name is the boat. The waves stay; you float. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, saloks on crossing the terrifying ocean, e.g. salok 12, 'bhau nidh utrahi paar' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427–1428)
